2. The appellants' case in the that the disputed lands were thrown up in the bed of the river Jhurjhuria as char lands lying to the contiguous north of the two mouzas known as Kanchi Harania and Shankar Kati within P.S. Shamnagar District Khulna that in 1953 when the said char became fit for cultivation, the Government of East Pakistan started Settlement Case No. 9/53-54 for settle went of the said char lands, that Appellant No. 1 having applied for settlement of the land on behalf of all the appellants, the Khas Mahal Officer proposed to settle the disputed land permanently with them by his order dated 8-7-53, which was duly approved by the Collector of Khulna and subsequently also by the Board of Revenue, that Appellant No. 1 paid the Salami money and rent to the Government and executed a Kabuliyat on 15.9.53 in favour of the Collector of Khulna, who accepted the same, that the area of the land under settlement measured 18.34 acres, which subsequently increased to 27.63 acres by accretion, that this entire 27.63 acres of land were wrongly recorded in the Khas Khatian of Respondents No. 2 to 4 that after the acquisition of the rent receiving interests and the excess Khas lands of the said Respondents they said lands had been suit was recorded in the Khas Khatian of the Government, Respondent No. 1, that the Government Tahshilder settled some of the lands described in Schedule B to the plaint with the local cultivators, who had cut away the paddy grown by the appellants in the said lands and that the Government, Respondent No. 1, had been threatening to dispossess the appellants from the lands of Schedule A also. 

 3. The suit was contested by the Government, Respondent No. 1, claiming that the disputed lands were the Khas lands of respondent Nos. 2 to 4, the ex-rent receivers, that Khas Mahal Officer had no right to settle the disputed lands with the appellants. that the said lands were cultivated by the bargadars of respondents No. 2 to 4, that these lands were subsequently acquired by the Government under the provisions of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and that the Government had been in possession of the said lands since 1st Baisakh, 1362 B.S. 

 5. On appeal a Bench of the High Court Division came to the finding that the lands in suit were the Khas lands of Defendant No. 2 to 4 and as such the settlement granted on behalf of the Government was ultra vires the officers granting such settlement. It was further held that the appellants' claim to Schedule B as accretion to their lands in Schedule A would fail as their claim of settlement of Schedule A had failed and also because of the provisions of Presidents' Order No. 137 of 1972 under which the right of accretion granted to the private individuals under the general law was purported to have been taken away. It having been argued before the High Court Division that the Officers of the Government having specially granted settlement of the lands in Schedule. A as Government Khas lands and the Government having subsequently acquired title to the said lands, the law of estoppels would apply and that the Government would be stopped from asserting that it had no title to the said lands at the time when the settlement was granted. The learned Judges of the High Court Division negative the said plea on holding that the law of estoppels would not be attracted to the instant case. The appellants having put into evidence certain deeds of sale executed by the appellants in favour of certain strangers respecting the disputed lands which were marked as Exits. 10(a), 10(b), 10(c) and 10 (d) for the purpose of showing that the appellants exercised their right of possession in respect of the said lands. The High Court Division held that the vendees of the said deeds Exits. 10 series, having acquired interest in the disputed lands were necessary parties in the suit and that the said suit was not maintainable in their absence. The judgment and decree of the trial Court were set aside and the suit was dismissed on the basis of the aforesaid findings. 

 8. As regards the point’s No. 3 and 4, as have been set out above, they do not seem to be of much consequence in view of the findings arrived at by the High Court Division in the appeal before it. Having regard to pleadings of the parties and the evidence adduced, it appears that the learned Judges of the High Court Division were correct in applying the law of accretion in favour of defendant's No. 2 to 4's title to the lands in suit. The averments in the plaint itself show that the disputed Schedule A lands were char lands thrown up by the fluvial action of the river Jhur Jhuria as a gradual alluvial formation contiguous of two mouzas, namely, Kachi Harania and Shankar Kati. The riparian lands of the said two mouzas having appertained to the Khas lands of Defendants No. 2 to 4, these alluvial lands, as described in Schedule A, became the property of the said defendants in the same right as they had in the riparian lands under the provisions of Section 4 of Allusion and Diluvion Regulation (Bengal Regulation X( of 1825) and in conformity to the principle laid down by the Judicial Committee in Lopez vs. Muddan Mohan 13 M.I A. 567. So no exception can be taken to the said view of the High Court Division on this point. 

 9. As regards point No. 4 the High Court Division did not appear to have expressed any view to the effect that a tenancy of any agricultural land could not be founded on the basis of a Kabuliyat or payment of rent accepted or behalf of the landlord, but expressed a doubt, whether In the facts of the case, the settlement granted in respect of Schedule A lands by the Khas Mahal Office was duly approved by the Board of Revenue. 

 10. The decision of the learned Judges, however, was based on the finding that the Government having not had any right, title or interest in the Schedule A lands at the time when the purported settlement had been made, no title was created in favour of the plaintiffs on the basis of the said settlement. The relevant findings of the High Court Division in substance are that the newly formed lands, as described in Schedule A, being the khas lands of defendants No. 3 to 4, the Government did not acquire any title to the said lands before 14.4.55 and Oat the Officers of the Government had no authority to settle the said lands with the plaintiffs on the basis of the Kabuliyat Exhibit 2, executed on 15.9.53 and on the basis of the receipts Exits. 4 and 4 (a) for the payment of salami and Ext. 5, the receipt for the payment of rent. According to the learned Judges, the alleged settlement on the basis of the Kabuliyat was consequently ultra vires the officer concerned. 

 12. The Khas Mahal Office also correctly understood that the requisite approval was granted by the Board in its said letter, as it appears from the information supplied by the Khas Mahal Office on 8-10-55 on the application for information, also marked Ext. 1, which is to the following effect; "Settlement made in settlement Case No. 9/53-54 has been approved by the Board in their Memo No. 2344 GE dated 30-3-55". But even if the settlement had been meticulously regular, the plaintiffs could not claim any relief on the basis of the settlement in view of the finding (which cannot be said to have been wrong) that the Government on whose behalf the settlement was made having not acquired any right to the disputed land at the time of the said settlement, no right of tenancy vested in the plaintiffs on the basis of the said settlement. 

 18. The Government, defendant No. 1, contested the plaintiffs' claim with regard to Schedule A lands on the assertion that the Government did not acquire any right, title and interest in the said lands until 14-4-55 and therefore the plaintiffs did not acquire any interest in the disputed lands on the basis of the said settlement. The trial Court decreed the plaintiffs' suit on the finding that the Government was the full owner of the disputed lands at the time of granting settlement and that the plaintiffs did acquire the necessary title to the said lands on the basis of the settlement pleaded in the plaint. The High Court Division, however, on appeal found that the disputed lands were the khas lands of Defendants No. 2 to 4 at the time of the settlement pleaded by the plaintiffs and the Government did not have any title or interest therein until 14-4-55 when the same was acquired by the Government under the provisions of The East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and that as such the plaintiffs did not acquire any title on the basis of the settlement dated 15-9-53 when the Government had no right, title and interest in the said lands. 

 19. Having regard to the said view of the matter, an alternative argument based on the law of estoppels was advanced on behalf of the plaintiffs. Such argument does not appear to have been based on any new allegation of fact. The only question is whether on the facts proved the law of feeding the estoppels is attracted is any way. It is in the averments made in the plaint that the Government started a settlement Case No. 9/53-54 professedly for the settlement of Schedule A lands, obviously claiming they said lands to be the Government khas lands. The representation that the Government was authorized to transfer such lands as required under section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act is clear. Such a representation may have been made by the officer concerned on behalf of the Government erroneously, if not fraudulently. It is also in the averments made in the plaint that the Government, as a matter of fact, purported to transfer the said lands in favour of the plaintiffs on the basis of the Kabuliyat dated 15-9-53 as well as on the basis of payment of premium and rent in respect of the settlement of the said lands. This fact fulfills the second condition, as required under section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act. It is in the written statement that the Government had no right, title and interest in the disputed lands on 15-9-53, when the settlement was granted in favor of the plaintiffs, that the said lands were the khas lands of defendants No. 2 to 4 and that the Government subsequently acquired the right, title and interest of the said defendants in the disputed lands on 14-4-55 under the provisions of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. These allegations fulfill the 3rd consideration required by law of feeding the estoppel, as referred to above. These allegations have been found to be true by the High Court Division. In the context of the pleadings of the parties, as mentioned above, and the findings arrived at by the High Court Division, the plaintiffs cannot reasonably be debarred from invoking the law of feeding the estoppel in the alternative to their case in the plaint on the ground that they had not pleaded the law of estoppel in their plaint. The said law will apply perforce to the facts of the case, as proved on the basis of the respective pleadings. The plaintiffs having sued the Government for declaration of their title to schedule A lands on the basis of the settlement dated 15-9-53 may very well be said to have exercised their option to operate their settlement of schedule A lands on the title acquired by the Government subsequently under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, as provided in section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act. The learned judges of the High Court Division are not correct in taking the view that there was no definite and unambiguous representation on behalf of the Government and that whatever representation was made by the plaintiffs. The Order Sheet of the Settlement Case No. 9/53-54 which has been marked as Ext. 8(A) shows that the said case was started on 26-6-53 and the petition of the party seeking settlement was filed on 28-6-53. On 15-9-53 a kabuliyat was executed by the plaintiff No. 1 in favour of the Government stating the subject matter of the kabuliyat to the land appertaining to Khas Mahal. The approval of the Additional Deputy Collector and subsequently that of the Board of Revenue was given to the said settlement on the basis that the said lands were the Government khas lands. Obviously the Government officers, who were authorized to deal with Government khas mahal lands, erroneously thought that the disputed lands were part of the Government khas mahal and as such they were authorized to transfer the said lands to suitable individuals. On the said basis they started Settlement Case No. 9/53-54 avowedly for making settlement of the said Government Khas Mahal lands. The intending candidate, namely, plaintiff No. 1, naturally believed on the basis of the said representation that the Government was the clear owner of the said lands and acting under the said belief he sought the settlement of the same and paid money to the Government officers concerned on executing the necessary Kabuliyat. The Government officers in their turn accepted the said Kabuliyat and also received the money paid by the said plaintiff. It having been found by the Government that it had subsequently required the right, title and interest of Schedule A lands under the provisions provisions of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act and it having been so found also by the High Court Division, the transfer effected by the Kabuliyat Ext. 2 must operate on the right, title and interest of the Government which was subsequently acquired under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in terms of the provision of section 43 of the Transfer of the Property Act. The question of the settlement being ultra vires the Government Officers concerned has no bearing on the application of the provision of section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act. It may be said to have been ultra vires of the Government officer in the sense that the lands in question having been not the Government Property, the Government officers were not authorized to transfer the same and no title accrued in favour of the plaintiffs on the basis of such transfer. But the Government having subsequently acquired title to the said trans ferried lands there is no bar to the application of the law of feeding the estoppels.
